clue.text: Teams exist first, what's more

indicators.note: first tells us the word for exist goes at the front of the word for teams

parts.note: to exist is simply to be
teams in a match are the sides

explanation.surface: A sports writer insists that the squads must be there before anything else happens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first' puts BE ahead of SIDES rather than after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are adverbs adding a further point, as in 'moreover'.

clue.text: Bee came indistinctly into view and flower opened

parts.note: B is how the letter bee is written
to loom is to appear dimly and threateningly

explanation.surface: A bee hovered into sight as a blossom unfurled.
explanation.definitionFit: A plant that flowered has put out its blossom, as a rose opens.

clue.text: It's not exactly a seat on the board he wants he just likes the sport of standing for it

definitions.text: It's not exactly a seat on the board he wants he just likes the sport of standing for it

parts.words: It's not exactly a seat on the board he wants he just likes the sport of standing for it
parts.note: the language of boardrooms and elections, seats and standing, is reread as someone balancing upright on a board on the waves

explanation.surface: A candidate who stands for a board seat purely for the fun of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Standing for a seat on the board' suggests a company election; here the board is a surfboard and he stands on it.
explanation.definitionFit: A rider of waves on a board, the sportsman who stands upright as the breaker carries him.

clue.text: Evil genius lurking inside a retrograde monarch

indicators.note: lurking inside means the answer is concealed within the letters of the words that follow

explanation.surface: A wicked mastermind is secretly at work inside a backward-looking king.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs across 'retrograDE MONarch'. 'retrograde' looks like a reversal signal but is only fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A malign spirit or evil genius in the old sense, an attendant spirit leading someone astray.

clue.text: Surely, there was a time I might have trod the heights" (Oscar Wilde).

definitions.text: Surely, there was a time I might have trod the heights" (Oscar Wilde).

parts.words: Surely, there was a time I might have trod the heights" (Oscar Wilde)
parts.note: a line from Wilde's sonnet Hélas! with the adjective before heights left out, to be supplied by the solver

explanation.surface: A quotation from Oscar Wilde regretting a lost chance of greatness.
explanation.walkthrough: Wilde's sonnet 'Hélas!' reads 'Surely there was a time I might have trod / The ___ heights'; the missing word is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Wilde pictures the summits bathed in daylight, the bright heights of achievement he might have reached.

clue.text: Failure of a pigeon

definitions.meaning: to come a ... is to fall heavily or fail badly
a breed of fancy pigeon with a large crop, like the pouter

explanation.surface: A racing pigeon that never makes it home.
explanation.definitionFit: A heavy fall or flop is a cropper, and the same word names a pouter-like breed of domestic pigeon.

clue.text: Saw a peevish act of unkindness

parts.note: peevish means cross
a cut is a hurtful snub or unkind act

explanation.surface: Someone witnessed an irritable, hurtful slight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saw' looks like the past tense of 'see', but it is the tool: a crosscut saw cuts across the grain.
explanation.definitionFit: A crosscut is a saw made for cutting wood across the grain.

clue.text: Gives too much importance to the speed at which the fielders get through 'their work?

definitions.meaning: values something more highly than it deserves

definitions.text: speed at which the fielders get through 'their work
definitions.meaning: in cricket, the number of six-ball sets bowled per hour by a fielding side; the plural answer stands for the rates of several sides

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether the pace of cricket fielding is given undue weight.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket an 'over' is a set of six balls, and the over rate measures how quickly a fielding side bowls them.
explanation.definitionFit: To exaggerate the worth of something; also, in cricket, the measured pace of bowling by a fielding team.

clue.text: Catch a piano. falling over-get the plate that falls from it too!

indicators.note: falling over means the whole run of pieces is turned upside down, read from the end

parts.note: a net is used to catch fish
p is the musical abbreviation for piano, softly

explanation.surface: Someone drops a piano and the dish balanced on it crashes down too.
explanation.walkthrough: 'falling over' turns NET + A + P into the answer. A paten is the small plate used for bread at the Eucharist.
explanation.definitionFit: A shallow dish, usually of silver or gold, holding the communion bread.

clue.text: Stormy petrel going to the east a very full clue!

indicators.note: stormy suggests turbulence, so the letters of the bird's name are tossed about

explanation.surface: A storm petrel flies eastward, and the setter boasts of a well-packed clue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stormy' rearranges PETREL into REPLET, and E for east follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Filled to capacity or well supplied, like a diner who has eaten plenty.

clue.text: He's trying not to catch crabs!

definitions.text: He's trying not to catch crabs!

parts.words: He's trying not to catch crabs
parts.note: to catch a crab is the rowing mishap of jamming a blade in the water, so this man is at the oars, not on the beach

explanation.surface: A man on the seashore anxiously avoiding the crustaceans.
explanation.walkthrough: The crabs suggest a beach or fishing, but catching a crab is a rower's error.
explanation.definitionFit: A rower in a crew dreads the stroke that snags his blade, known in rowing slang as catching a crab.

clue.text: But did 'people ever get very far with this dance?

definitions.text: But did 'people ever get very far with this dance?

parts.words: But did 'people ever get very far with this dance
parts.note: the name of this old ballroom dance suggests a single pace, which would hardly take anyone far

explanation.surface: A sceptic wonders whether dancers ever covered much ground in this routine.
explanation.walkthrough: The one-step was a brisk early twentieth-century ballroom dance; the joke is reading its name literally.
explanation.definitionFit: A fast ballroom dance of the 1910s, popular alongside the foxtrot and named for its single walking step per beat.

clue.text: A crime ruins Anne, perhaps but shouldn't this 'have safeguarded her, in the main?

definitions.text: shouldn't this 'have safeguarded her, in the main?

indicators.note: perhaps signals that the letters of the preceding words may be arranged differently

explanation.surface: A ship called Anne is wrecked through foul play, and someone asks why her policy did not protect her.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges A CRIME RUINS ANNE. Anne is a ship, and 'the main' is the open sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Cover against loss of a vessel or cargo at sea is exactly what an owner buys to protect a ship on the ocean.

clue.text: Strange to see a: Communist going round about — enough to make you tremble!

indicators.note: going round means the turned word for Communist encloses the word for strange
about here means turned the other way round, so the word for Communist reads backwards

parts.note: a Communist is a Red
strange means odd

explanation.surface: Seeing a Communist circling about is enough to give anyone the shakes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' turns RED into DER, and 'going round' puts ODD inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: To dodder is to totter or shake unsteadily, typically from age or weakness.

clue.text: Expert in money matters is not come to ruin

indicators.note: to ruin means the words before it are wrecked and rebuilt in a new order

explanation.surface: A financial adviser insists he has not been brought to bankruptcy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to ruin' rearranges IS NOT COME.
explanation.definitionFit: A specialist in finance and the production of wealth, the study of how money and resources behave.

clue.text: Repeated with some stores

definitions.meaning: repeated many times, numerous or manifold
a chain of shops under one name is called a ... store, or simply a ...

explanation.surface: Something said again and again among a few shops.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a multiple is a retail chain such as a supermarket group with many branches.
explanation.definitionFit: Manifold or occurring many times; and as a British noun, a chain store with many branches.

clue.text: Walk in concerted fashion?

parts.note: concerted hints at a kind of concert at which audiences once strolled, and a leisurely stroll shares that name

explanation.surface: Several people stroll together in step.
explanation.walkthrough: A prom, short for promenade concert, is a concert where the audience may stand or walk about, as at the BBC Proms in London.
explanation.definitionFit: A leisurely stroll taken for pleasure, and also a concert at which listeners could walk around.

clue.text: Share in the exploit, then quit

indicators.note: in means the word for share is placed inside the word for exploit

parts.note: an exploit is a deed
a part is a share

explanation.surface: Someone took their portion of a daring scheme and then walked away.
explanation.definitionFit: Left or went away, both past tenses of leaving a place.

clue.text: A' don more eccentric becomes completely, isolated from the world

indicators.note: eccentric means odd or off-centre, so the letters before it are to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An increasingly eccentric university lecturer ends up cut off from society altogether.
explanation.walkthrough: 'eccentric' rearranges A DON MORE. The printed apostrophe after A is a stray mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone stranded with no contact, like a sailor put ashore on a desert island, is left utterly alone.

clue.text: One way to hold hands

parts.note: holding hands sounds romantic, but here the wrists are held fast by a fetter

explanation.surface: Advice on how couples might link fingers.
explanation.walkthrough: Hand-holding suggests sweethearts; the device actually binds a prisoner's hands.
explanation.definitionFit: A fetter for the wrist, a handcuff, literally restrains the hands.

clue.text: Idiot!.That greasy liquid must be dirty!

parts.note: an idiot is an ass
oil is a greasy liquid

explanation.surface: Someone scolds a fool for letting oily fluid get grimy.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is an archaic verb; one old sense is to sully, though it more often meant to absolve.
explanation.definitionFit: An obsolete verb meaning to soil or sully, as well as its better-known archaic sense of pardoning.

clue.text: Went to bed. to the accompaniment of a song with Irish associations

parts.note: a lay is a song or ballad
Down is a county in Northern Ireland

explanation.surface: Someone retired for the night while an Irish ballad played.
explanation.walkthrough: County Down is one of the six counties of Northern Ireland, home of the Mountains of Mourne.
explanation.definitionFit: To go to bed is to recline for sleep, the past tense of lying down.

clue.text: A barrier's made of stones

parts.note: a gate is a barrier; the possessive 's supplies the final S

explanation.surface: A fence is built from rocks.
explanation.definitionFit: Ornamental semi-precious stones, banded forms of chalcedony.

clue.text: Picture palace in Trafalgar Square?

parts.note: a picture palace sounds like an old cinema, but here it is a grand building full of paintings on that London square

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether there is a cinema in central London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Picture palace' is old British slang for a cinema; the paintings here are the real pictures.
explanation.definitionFit: Britain's principal public collection of paintings stands on the north side of Trafalgar Square in London.

clue.text: That place in another European country:

indicators.note: in means the answer sits within the letters of the words that follow

explanation.surface: A location in a foreign country within Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs across 'anoTHER European'.
explanation.definitionFit: An adverb pointing to a location away from the speaker, the opposite of here.

clue.text: Obviously not half a pint only of lager!

indicators.note: only of means the answer is made up purely of the letters of the following word, rearranged

explanation.surface: A drinker insists that a small measure of beer will not do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'only of' rearranges LAGER. In a British pub a 'large' is a full pint, as opposed to a half.
explanation.definitionFit: A full pint is a big measure of beer, clearly more than a half.

clue.text: In the course of one revolving moon, Was fiddler statesman and buffoon (Dryden)

definitions.text: In the course of one revolving moon, Was fiddler statesman and buffoon (Dryden)

parts.words: In the course of one revolving moon, Was fiddler statesman and buffoon
parts.note: a couplet from Dryden's portrait of Zimri in Absalom and Achitophel with one of the listed callings left out, to be supplied by the solver

explanation.surface: A quotation from Dryden mocking a man who changed careers every month.
explanation.walkthrough: The line in Dryden reads 'Was ___, fiddler, statesman, and buffoon'; the missing first calling is the answer, an old spelling of which was 'chymist'.
explanation.definitionFit: Dryden's fickle Zimri tried alchemy and science, listed as one more calling beside music, politics and clowning.

clue.text: Such rent trouble is a big blow

parts.note: rent, as a past participle, means torn
ado means fuss or trouble

explanation.surface: A tenant laments that this rent dispute is a serious setback.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rent' looks like the payment for a home, but here it is the past participle of 'rend', to tear.
explanation.definitionFit: A violent rotating windstorm is about as strong a gust of wind as there is.

clue.text: Made the pick of a really select edition

indicators.note: of here means the answer is taken out of the run of letters in the words that follow

explanation.surface: A book was chosen as the best of an exclusive printing.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs across 'sELECT EDition'.
explanation.definitionFit: Chose by vote or by preference, as when voters pick a candidate.

clue.text: Haggard heroine 'lived in low and illegal dive

parts.note: She is the title character of H. Rider Haggard's novel 'She'
been, as in 'has been', stands for has lived or existed

explanation.surface: A gaunt heroine once lived in a seedy drinking den.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Haggard' looks like 'gaunt', but it is the novelist H. Rider Haggard. A shebeen is an unlicensed Irish or Scottish drinking house.
explanation.definitionFit: An unlicensed bar selling drink without permission, originally in Ireland, is a disreputable drinking den.
